about.title: Point-Slope and Standard Form
audience: Follows 8th-grade math and the earlier lessons on slope and slope-intercept form
about.length_note: This class is a little over 30 minutes. It teaches two new forms plus the conversions between them, and each idea gets its own example and check. It is easy to pause after beat 7 (point-slope done) and pick up again at beat 8 (standard form).

say.text: Last class you wrote lines as y = mx + b. Today we add two more ways to write the same line.

show.text: Two new ways to write a line: point-slope and standard form

say.text: First, point-slope form. Use it when you know the slope and just one point on the line, any point.
Here m is the slope. The pair (x₁, y₁) is the point. It comes from the slope formula, with the fraction cleared away.

show.text:
m = the slope
(x₁, y₁) = a point on the line
x and y stay as letters

ask.q: In y − 5 = 2(x − 3), what is the slope?
ask.why: The slope m is the number multiplying the (x − x₁) part. Here that is 2. The point is (3, 5).

say.text: Example. Sam has 50 gems after 2 hours of play, and he earns 15 gems an hour. The point is (2, 50) and the slope is 15.

ask.q: A line has slope 4 and goes through (1, 9). Which is its point-slope form?
ask.why: Slope 4 goes in front of the bracket. The point (1, 9) gives y − 9 and x − 1, with y first.

say.text: Watch the signs. The form has minus signs in it, so a negative coordinate turns the minus into a plus.

ask.q: Which is the point-slope form for slope 3 through (−2, 4)?
ask.why: x − (−2) becomes x + 2. The y-coordinate 4 stays positive, so it is y − 4.

say.text: You can turn point-slope into slope-intercept. Spread the slope over the bracket, then get y alone.

ask.q: Rewrite y − 1 = 3(x − 2) as y = mx + b.
ask.why: 3(x − 2) = 3x − 6. Add 1 to both sides and you get 3x − 5.

say.text: Quick check that the line really goes through the point. Put the point into the equation and see if both sides match. For y = 2x − 1 and (3, 5): 2·3 − 1 = 5. Yes.
New form. Standard form puts the x-term and the y-term together on one side, and a plain number on the other.

ask.q: Which equation is in standard form?
ask.why: Standard form has x and y on the left and just a number on the right. The others are slope-intercept or point-slope.

say.text: Before using it, a word we need: intercepts. They are the spots where the line crosses the axes.

show.text:
x-intercept: crosses the x-axis, looks like (a, 0)
y-intercept: crosses the y-axis, looks like (0, b)

ask.q: What is always true about the y-coordinate of an x-intercept?
wrong: It is the same as x
ask.why: On the x-axis you are zero units up or down, so y = 0. That is why x-intercepts look like (a, 0).

say.text: Standard form makes intercepts easy. For the x-intercept, set y = 0. For the y-intercept, set x = 0. Then solve.

ask.why: Set y = 0: 4x = 16, so x = 4. Set x = 0: 2y = 16, so y = 8.

say.text: Now graph it. Plot the two intercepts and draw a line through them. A third point is a safety check.

show.text: A coordinate grid. The line 2x + 3y = 12 crosses the x-axis at (6, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 4). A third dot at (3, 2) sits on the same line.

ask.right: To check that all three points line up
wrong: Because a line needs three points
ask.why: Two points are enough to draw a line. A third that lines up tells you that you did not make a mistake.

say.text: A common mix-up: C is not the y-intercept. It only is when B equals 1.

ask.why: Set x = 0: 5y = 10, so y = 2. (5, 0) is the x-intercept, not the y-intercept.

say.text: Next, convert. Standard to slope-intercept: get y alone.

ask.q: Rewrite x + 2y = 8 as y = mx + b.
ask.why: Subtract x: 2y = −x + 8. Divide everything by 2: y = −(1/2)x + 4.

say.text: Point-slope to standard: spread, then move x and y to one side. Many books want whole numbers with A positive.

ask.q: What is y − 5 = 2(x − 3) in standard form, with A positive?
ask.why: Spread: y − 5 = 2x − 6. Move terms: −2x + y = −1. Multiply by −1: 2x − y = 1. The last choice is slope-intercept form.

say.text: If the slope is a fraction, multiply by the bottom number to clear it. Slope 1/2 through (4, 1).

ask.q: Write y = (1/3)x + 2 in standard form with whole numbers and A positive.
ask.why: Multiply by 3: 3y = x + 6. Move terms: −x + 3y = 6. Multiply by −1: x − 3y = −6.

say.text: Two special lines fit too. x = 4 is a vertical line through 4 on the x-axis. y = 3 is a horizontal line through 3 on the y-axis.

show.text:
x = a: vertical line
y = b: horizontal line

ask.q: What does the graph of x = 5 look like?
ask.right: A vertical line crossing the x-axis at 5
wrong: A horizontal line crossing the y-axis at 5
ask.why: Every point on x = 5 has x equal to 5 and any y. That stacks up into a vertical line.

say.text: So which form should you pick? Match the form to what you are told.

show.text:
Slope and y-intercept → y = mx + b
Slope and a point → y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Two amounts that add to a total, or fast graphing → Ax + By = C

ask.q: You know a line has slope 4 and passes through (1, 9). Which form is the fastest to write?
wrong: Slope-intercept form, with no other steps
None of them can be used
ask.why: The slope and a point are exactly what point-slope form asks for. You can still convert later if you want y = mx + b.

say.text: Standard form is good for budgets. A game shop sells tickets for 4 coins and snacks for 3 coins. You spend exactly 24 coins.

ask.q: If you buy no tickets, how many snacks can you buy with 24 coins?
ask.why: No tickets means x = 0. So 3y = 24 and y = 8. That is the y-intercept (0, 8). The x-intercept (6, 0) is 6 tickets and no snacks.

say.text: That is the class. Point-slope needs a slope and a point. Standard form gives easy intercepts. You can convert between all three.

show.text:
Point-slope: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Standard: Ax + By = C
Intercepts: set y = 0, then x = 0
Convert by spreading, moving terms, or clearing fractions

notes.topic: Point-slope form comes from the slope formula; the course standard HSA-CED.A.2 asks students to create equations in two variables and graph them with labels and scales (see s9).
Writing a line from two points uses point-slope form too; that is practised next class.
Standard form is used again when solving systems by elimination.

other_side.claim: Standard form must have whole-number A, B and C, with A positive.
other_side.other_view: Books differ. One university text says A, B and C are integers and A is usually positive. A high-school text says they can be any real numbers, as long as A and B are not both zero. Follow your own teacher's or test's rule.

other_side.claim: Slope-intercept form is the best form for real-world problems.
other_side.other_view: OpenStax notes that most applications of linear equations use slope-intercept form. But it also says intercepts are often the quickest way to graph a line, and standard form gives them directly. Which is best depends on what the problem gives you and asks for.
